title: Title and context
short: Written at Lady Gregory's Coole Park in 1916–17, published in the Little Review (June 1917) and as the title poem of Yeats's 1917 and 1919 volumes.
body: Coole Park, County Galway, was the estate of Yeats's friend and patron Augusta, Lady Gregory, where he spent summers from 1897 onward. The poem was written between 1916 and early 1917, first published in the Little Review in June 1917, and became the title poem of The Wild Swans at Coole (Cuala Press, 1917; Macmillan, 1919). Its context includes Yeats's sense of ageing (he was fifty-one), his renewed and rejected proposal to Maud Gonne in 1916, and his feeling for Iseult Gonne; critics such as Daniel Tobin also set it against the Irish unrest of the time. The swans of the lake are real, but the poem gives them symbolic weight.

title: Stanza form
short: Five six-line stanzas with lines of varied length (four, three, four, three, five, three stresses), rhymed abcbdd.
body: Each stanza has an unusual pattern of stresses: lines 1 and 3 roughly tetrameter, lines 2, 4 and 6 trimeter, line 5 pentameter, with rhymes abcbdd. The first stanza's closing couplet is a half-rhyme ('stones / swans'), a muted close, though later couplets ('rings / wings', 'head / tread') rhyme fully. The movement is meditative and conversational, with long sentences carried over the short lines, a style Yeats developed in this period as he moved from the ornate manner of his early verse to a more spare, spoken idiom.

anchor: Under the October twilight the water
title: October twilight
short: Autumn and twilight together suggest the end of the year and of the day, mirroring the poet's sense of ageing.
body: The setting fuses time of year and time of day: October twilight, a season and hour of decline. The water 'mirrors a still sky': the stillness and reflection of the lake create an image of calm and of contemplation. 'Brimming' water (full to the edge) contrasts with the 'dry' paths, a fullness in nature against a sense of loss in the speaker. The images of autumn are traditional in the elegiac lyric, from Keats's 'To Autumn' to Shakespeare's Sonnet 73.

title: nine and fifty swans
short: Fifty-nine is an odd number: since swans pair for life, one is left without a mate, often read as a figure for the solitary poet.
body: The archaic inverted numeral ('nine and fifty' for fifty-nine) gives the count a ballad-like, almost legendary tone. Many readers note that an odd number means one swan is unpaired, which casts the poet, unmarried and repeatedly refused by Maud Gonne, as the odd one out among the 'lover by lover' couples of stanza 4. Others caution against over-reading a number that may record a real count. The act of counting itself suggests an attempt to measure and possess what will escape.

title: The nineteenth Autumn
short: Yeats first visited Coole in 1897; he counts nineteen autumns since then and returns to the same scene.
body: Yeats's first extended stay at Coole was in the summer and autumn of 1897, a time of emotional exhaustion after years of unrequited love for Maud Gonne; Lady Gregory nursed him back to health and became a lifelong collaborator. The 'nineteenth Autumn' sets the poem's time scheme: two moments compared, then and now. (Counting 1897 as the first autumn the nineteenth would fall in 1915, while the poem was written in 1916, so the figure is approximate or counted loosely.) 'Come upon me' presents age as something that has overtaken him from outside. The numbers (nineteen, fifty-nine) give the poem a sense of exact record.

anchor: Since I first made my count
title: made my count
short: The act of counting the swans, a literal act and a figure for the poet's attempt to measure and hold experience.
body: In 1897 the speaker began to count the swans but they flew up before he had 'well finished'; the incompleteness of the count anticipates the poem's sense of the swans as elusive and beyond his control. The swans 'mount' and 'scatter wheeling in great broken rings': the circles anticipate Yeats's later symbol of the gyre, though that system was not developed until after his marriage in 1917 and A Vision (1925). The 'clamorous wings' introduce the sound of the swans, important in stanza 3.

title: great broken rings
short: The swans rise in incomplete circles, a recurrent Yeatsian image of motion and change.
body: The rings are 'broken': the swans form circles that open and disperse. Some critics see a prefiguration of the 'widening gyre' of 'The Second Coming' (1920); others read it more simply as precise observation of birds taking off. 'Wheeling' suggests the circular flight of birds and the turning wheel of time, a theme that runs through the poem. The image of broken rings may also hint at broken attachments, the poet's own unfulfilled love.

anchor: And now my heart is sore
title: my heart is sore
short: The poem's emotional centre: watching the beautiful creatures makes the speaker conscious of his own loss and ageing.
body: The 'brilliant creatures' (shining, radiant) make the poet's heart 'sore', grieved and aching. 'All's changed' is a crucial phrase in 1916: the same year Yeats wrote 'Easter, 1916', with its refrain 'All changed, changed utterly'. The private change (his heart has aged, his loves have failed) and the public change of the Rising are both in the background. The stanza contrasts the 'lighter tread' of the younger man in 1897 with the present weight of age.

title: bell-beat
short: A compound for the rhythmic, ringing sound of swans' wings in flight.
body: Swans in flight make a loud, throbbing, musical sound with their wings, which Yeats renders with the compound 'bell-beat'. The alliteration suggests both regularity (beat) and resonance (bell), and perhaps also a bell tolling, a hint of mortality. The memory of hearing that sound for the first time 'above my head' is linked to the young man's 'lighter tread', so that the sound becomes a measure of the change in him.

title: lover by lover
short: The swans swim in pairs; swans traditionally mate for life, an emblem of constancy the poet lacks.
body: Swans were long proverbial for fidelity, and the observation that they pair for life underlies the phrase 'lover by lover'. The adjective 'Unwearied' contrasts the swans with the weary poet. 'Companionable streams' is a transferred epithet: the swans are companionable, and so, in their eyes, is the water. The swans seem to escape time ('Their hearts have not grown old'), although individual swans die; Yeats treats them as a species or an idea, unchanging in a way the poet cannot be. The stanza ends with 'Passion or conquest' attending on them.

title: Passion or conquest
short: Love and the pursuit or winning of love (and perhaps achievement) still 'attend upon' the swans wherever they go.
body: 'Attend upon' means accompany as servants: passion and conquest follow the swans as attendants follow nobility. 'Conquest' may refer to winning a mate (amorous conquest) and, more broadly, to the energy of achievement. The phrase defines what the poet feels he has lost: the capacity for passion and the success of conquest in love. 'Wander where they will' stresses the swans' freedom, against the speaker's own fixedness at the same lake after nineteen years.

title: the still water
short: The swans resting on the still lake: the image of the opening returns, now 'mysterious' and about to vanish.
body: The final stanza returns to the calm of stanza 1, with 'still water' echoing the 'still sky' and the 'Unwearied still' of stanza 4: Yeats exploits 'still' as both 'motionless' and 'yet, even now'. 'Mysterious, beautiful' isolates two adjectives on one line, suspending the movement. The swans' stillness becomes enigmatic, as the speaker imagines them building nests elsewhere, delighting other men's eyes in the future.

title: when I awake some day / To find they have flown away
short: The ending is ambiguous: the swans may leave, or the poet may lose the power to see or feel them, or the line may glance at death.
body: The poem ends with a question. Readers propose several meanings: literal (the swans will one day migrate or move elsewhere); psychological (the poet will 'awake' to find that his capacity for wonder and passion has gone); or mortal (death as an awakening). Some critics read 'awake' as waking from a dream, so that the swans may be a vision that the poet will lose. The question form refuses closure, which suits the poem's theme of impermanence. The phrase 'Delight men's eyes' implies a future in which others, not he, will enjoy the beauty.
